script: We reverse gazumped a greedy landlord and it was glorious.. Gazumping occurs when an agent or seller accepts an offer you make to buy a property at an agreed price but the property is sold to someone else. I'd been living that nightmare for fifteen years, and honestly, it was the proudest thing I've ever pulled off. My bestie, her hubby, and their five kids were stuck in an old four‑bed house in a pricey city, paying $400 a week. The kitchen was a dumpster, the drains were a biohazard, but they made it work. The owner was a sweet old lady, super rich, and she'd frozen the rent for five years, promising them a chance to buy once they hit a loan. She was like a landlord‑angel, so they trusted her and saved every cent. But then—two days after they told her they were ready—the old lady died, and nothing was written down. (I know, right?) Enter her four kids: mega‑wealthy, portfolio‑obsessed, and they said the sale would go through once probate finished. I thought, "Cool, this is still solid." But here's the thing: they were holding the house hostage, waiting to raise the price. While I was stuck watching my friends make a few cosmetic changes, they were lining up a new plan. They'd upped the asking price by $80,000 and put the place on the open market. The open house was in a week, and with the market hot, it would sell fast. I felt the stakes climb—my friends could lose their home, maybe get evicted, and there were barely any affordable two‑bed options. If they failed, they'd be staring at a future of rent hikes. What I didn't know was that the landlords had a long‑term agenda: to squeeze a few thousand out of a struggling family, and they were all about that greedy vibe. So while they scrambled for cash, I started plotting. And that's when everything changed. --- So here's what happened next. I started the sabotage plan, and it was pure Gen Z genius. We needed the house to look like a nightmare without making my friends look bad. First, we over‑decorated. I ripped wallpaper, painted bright colors, and hung motorcycle memorabilia everywhere. The place felt cramped, like a shoebox. But here's the thing: the smell had to kill too. I boiled a head of cabbage on the stove, sprayed ammonia around the doors, and dumped two dozen rotten eggs down the drain. The sewer gas hit like a punch. The neighbors? We staged a crime scene. I got a moldy couch and dumped it in the front yard of the neighbor across the street, with their permission of course. And what I didn't know was that the street would turn into a circus on the open day. We called every car‑owner friend with a loud, crappy ride. They drove laps around the block during the open house, turning traffic into a rave. The rugby club joined in—big guys in rough gear, motorcycles revving, and a BBQ set up next door. They brought free food and cheap beer, turning the neighborhood into a party zone. The open house was a madhouse. People came in and out in minutes. A lady sat in her car, watched the chaos, and drove away. One bloke who stayed was brave enough to chat with a leaving partygoer. He asked if this was a regular thing, and the answer was, "Every couple of weeks, we've got an after‑party morning and a night before." That guy also mentioned the drains that always smelled like tree roots. The potential buyer left with a face that said, "I am not buying this place." But here's the thing: my friends were the only ones who made an offer. They still had to pay more than they'd planned, but not as much as the greedy bastards wanted. They signed the papers and paid the deposit that day. And that's when the owners' faces turned to a mix of shock and disbelief. The brave buyer finally put in an offer $30,000 higher, but the anti‑gazumping laws sealed the deal. The landlords could do nothing. I'd love to see their faces when they realized I'd outsmarted them. Now, the truth: 2004 rent was $400, which was already high. By the time the old lady died, the average rent for a house that size had only risen by about $40. Today, those four‑bed houses in the area go for roughly $800 a week. And that's the tea, bestie. The battle was won, and my friends got the house they deserved, and the landlords got a taste of their own medicine.
